stories.headline: OIL JUMPS TO FIVE-MONTH HIGH AS HOUTHI ATTACKS RATTLE MIDDLE EAST, DOW SHEDS 600+ POINTS
stories.body: Brent crude surged toward $114-115 a barrel and WTI topped $100 after Houthi attacks inside Saudi Arabia revived fears of a wider regional disruption and renewed talk of U.S. strikes on Iran; the Dow fell 1.23% (-600+ pts) to 52,215.16 and the S&P 500 slipped 0.52% to 7,623.68 to close out Wall Street's roughest week since June. Markets are closed for the weekend, so this remains the most current read heading into the Fed's Tuesday-Wednesday meeting.
stories.explain: Oil's jump isn't about a confirmed supply loss yet — it's a risk premium, the price the market pays to insure against the chance that tanker routes near the Strait of Hormuz or Saudi export infrastructure actually get hit next. That premium gets priced into crude immediately through futures and options, long before a single barrel stops flowing, which is why Brent can spike 5%+ on an attack that caused no direct production outage. For equities, the read-through is twofold: higher energy costs squeeze corporate margins and consumer spending power, and a sustained oil spike complicates the Fed's inflation math right as it heads into a live rate decision this week.

stories.headline: COREWEAVE SLIDES ANOTHER 2.5% AS MORGAN STANLEY SLASHES PRICE TARGET TO $70
stories.body: CoreWeave shares fell to $54.24 (-2.46%) Friday, extending Thursday's 10% plunge to $55.60, after Morgan Stanley cut its price target to $70 from $99 — following Bernstein's cut to $51 from $74 a day earlier — as Wall Street keeps re-underwriting the roughly $51 billion in debt and lease obligations behind the AI-infrastructure buildout.
stories.explain: A price-target cut is an analyst publicly lowering their estimate of a company's discounted future cash flows, usually because new information (here, mounting doubt that CoreWeave's contracted cloud revenue can comfortably service its debt load) changes the risk embedded in that model. Two independent banks cutting targets within 24 hours signals the concern is spreading across sell-side desks, not confined to one skeptical analyst, and it reinforces the equity-market version of the same stress already visible in CoreWeave's deeply discounted bonds.

stories.headline: HOT INFLATION DATA REVIVES HAWKISH-FED WORRIES, 10-YEAR YIELD REBOUNDS TO 4.98%
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield bounced back to near 4.98% Friday, clawing back most of Thursday's sharp flight-to-safety drop, after hotter-than-expected inflation data pushed chipmakers like Nvidia lower and revived doubts about how much further the Fed can cut rates at Wednesday's decision.
stories.explain: Thursday's yield drop was a growth-and-credit scare — investors buying Treasuries because they feared AI-debt stress would slow the economy. Friday's rebound flips the driver to inflation: when a CPI-adjacent data point surprises to the upside, markets reprice the expected path of Fed policy toward fewer or later cuts, which pushes yields back up almost mechanically since bond prices move inversely to the rate future buyers will demand. Layering a fresh oil shock on top of that inflation surprise is exactly the combination that makes a central bank's job hardest: it can't cut aggressively into rising energy-driven inflation without risking its credibility on price stability.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIDES TOWARD $4,000 FOR A SECOND SESSION AS THE HAVEN TRADE BREAKS DOWN
stories.body: Gold fell roughly 0.75% to about $3,995 an ounce, its second straight decline and a more-than-two-month low, even as oil spiked on Middle East risk and equities wobbled — a divergence that shows real yields, not geopolitical fear, are currently setting the price.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its attractiveness is driven largely by the real (inflation-adjusted) interest rate: when nominal yields rise on hawkish-Fed repricing faster than inflation expectations do, the opportunity cost of holding zero-yield gold instead of Treasuries goes up, and gold gets sold even amid a geopolitical scare that would normally support it. That's the opposite mechanism from oil, where the risk premium is dominating; seeing gold and oil move in opposite directions on the same headline is a tell that this week's stress is being read as an inflation-and-rates story more than a pure flight-to-safety one.

stories.headline: APPLE BRIEFLY RECLAIMS TITLE OF WORLD'S MOST VALUABLE COMPANY FROM NVIDIA
stories.body: Apple's market capitalization briefly surpassed Nvidia's intraday Friday as investors rotated out of AI-infrastructure risk and into steadier, services-driven cash flows during the week's debt-fueled selloff in chip and cloud names.
stories.explain: When a sector carrying high leverage and capex risk (AI infrastructure) gets repriced lower, capital doesn't just disappear — it often rotates into comparably large companies seen as safer, like Apple, whose earnings depend more on recurring hardware upgrade cycles and services revenue than on debt-financed data-center bets. The swap in market-cap rankings is a visible, real-time snapshot of that rotation, and it tends to reverse quickly once the catalyst (here, CoreWeave-linked credit fear) stabilizes.

stories.headline: FLORIDA OPENS AS CONSENSUS NO. 1 DESPITE OVERTIME LOSS TO BAYLOR IN EXHIBITION
stories.body: Florida drew 47 of 59 first-place votes in the AP preseason poll and also topped the Coaches Poll, even after falling to Baylor 82-76 in overtime in its exhibition opener; Duke, Illinois, UConn and Arizona round out the AP top five, with preseason All-American Thomas Haugh leading the Gators into the Nov. 2-3 regular-season tip-off.

stories.headline: BEN SIMMONS TEARS ACHILLES AT PRACTICE, OUT FOR SEASON BEFORE KINGS DEBUT
stories.body: Simmons suffered a torn Achilles tendon in practice just days before his first regular-season appearance since 2024-25, ending his Kings season before it started, part of an early-season injury wave that also includes Magic forward Paolo Banchero's high-ankle sprain and Pistons center Jalen Duren's lower-body strain.

stories.headline: 49ERS' PERFECT SEASON ENDS AS FALCONS UPSET SAN FRANCISCO 29-20
stories.body: Atlanta snapped San Francisco's unbeaten start with a 29-20 win as Brock Purdy threw two interceptions, while the Buccaneers (2-5) throttled division-leading Carolina 43-13 behind Baker Mayfield and the Vikings improved to 6-0 by beating Indianapolis 16-10 in Sunday's Week 7 slate.

stories.headline: MIAMI ROUTS PITT 52-23, HURRICANES REACH NO. 1 FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2002
stories.body: Miami improved to 7-0 (5-0 ACC) behind Darian Mensah's 387 passing yards and four touchdowns and a school-record 16 catches from Malachi Toney, setting up the Hurricanes to open atop the AP poll when the first College Football Playoff rankings drop Nov. 3; BYU remains the sport's only other unbeaten power-conference team.

sports.detail: On a bye after beating Purdue 38-26 behind backup QB Elijah Brown (28-39, 251 yds, 3 TD) filling in for injured starter Demond Williams Jr. Next: at Nebraska, Sat. Oct. 31 (BTN) — Washington's first trip to Lincoln in 15 years and its first Big Ten meeting with the Huskers.

Closes out its exhibition slate today vs. Washington State (1 p.m. PT, Alaska Airlines Arena) after dropping its opener 109-91 at Boise State, where all five Husky starters fouled out. Regular-season opener: Sun., Nov. 2 vs. Colgate.

Host the unbeaten Chiefs (5-0) tonight on Sunday Night Football (5:20 p.m. PT, NBC) at 3-3, looking to snap a two-game skid; former Seahawk RB Kenneth Walker III, Seattle's Super Bowl MVP a year ago, returns to Lumen Field in Kansas City red.

Beat Miami 128-111 Friday to improve to 2-0, but lost Jalen Duren (right leg strain, re-eval in ~2 weeks) and Ausar Thompson (ankle, undisclosed) to injury; John Collins (23 pts) and Paul Reed (19 pts, 11 reb) picked up the slack. Next: at Philadelphia, tonight.

Still searching for Dan Wilson's replacement with a self-imposed Halloween target; Houston's Joe Espada is the top candidate now that his Astros contract has expired, with Carlos Correa among a reported 40-name list POBO Jerry Dipoto is considering.

deepDive.title: What the Fed's Dot Plot Actually Shows — and Why This Week's Meeting Doesn't Have One
content: This week's brief is dominated by a Fed decision that lands Wednesday with an unusually messy backdrop: a hot inflation print, a fresh oil shock from the Houthi attacks, and credit stress bleeding out of CoreWeave's AI-infrastructure debt. All of that would normally make investors turn to the Fed's "dot plot" for guidance on where rates are headed next. The catch is that October's meeting doesn't produce one — the Summary of Economic Projections is only released quarterly, in March, June, September and December. That makes Wednesday's statement language and Chair Kevin Warsh's press-conference tone the entire signal this week, carrying more weight than usual.

The dot plot itself is simple in construction but widely misread. At each quarterly meeting, all 19 FOMC participants (the seven Fed governors plus the presidents of the twelve regional Reserve Banks) anonymously plot where they expect the federal funds rate to sit at the end of the current year, each of the next two years, and in the "longer run." Each dot is one person's individual projection, not a commitment, and the median of those dots — not any vote — is the number markets fixate on as "the Fed's forecast." Only the rate-setting vote at that same meeting is binding; the dots are a snapshot of sentiment that the Fed itself is free to abandon by the very next meeting.

What most people miss is how fast that snapshot can move, and how little it actually binds future policy. In December 2021, the median dot showed roughly three quarter-point hikes for all of 2022. By March 2022, with inflation accelerating, the Fed had already raised once and the updated dots implied seven hikes for the year — a complete reversal within one quarter, based entirely on incoming data rather than any dot ever being "wrong" in a binding sense. That history is the reason serious market participants treat the dot plot as a conditional forecast, not a roadmap, and why a single hot CPI print — like the one that hit Friday — can scramble the expected path overnight.

Applied to this week: without a fresh SEP to anchor expectations, markets have to infer the Fed's reaction function from the statement's wording (does "elevated inflation" reappear, does "gradual" survive) and from how directly Warsh addresses the oil shock in his press conference. A hold with hawkish language would read as the Fed prioritizing the inflation scare over the CoreWeave-adjacent credit stress; a hold paired with dovish hedging on oil as "transitory" would signal the opposite. Either way, the next actual dot plot doesn't arrive until December, so Wednesday's words — not a chart — are what will move yields, gold, and the dollar this week.
